1.pericope_label: Hear ye the words of this covenant: cursed be the man that obeyeth not the words of this covenant

schools.summary: Dates the discourse from internal evidence to the reign of Josiah, maps the chapter's three parts, and shows the curse to be a mosaic of phrases from the newly discovered book of the Law.

Reads the plural summons as evidence of the few colleagues left to the prophet, and makes the appeal to the covenant a way of proving that the quarrel is not with Jeremiah but with Moses and with God.
Assigns the discourse to Zedekiah's first year, supposes the covenant may have been publicly read out, and sums the matter up in the blessing and curse from which God will not depart.
Frames the chapter as an indictment drawn up by a prosecutor, and opens the charter the people had forgotten, insisting that what God required was obedience rather than ceremony.

positions.view: the first year of Zedekiah, on a modern chronologer's authority
much earlier, probably under Josiah: the Chaldean invasion is not so near as in the chapter before, and the prophet still lives at Anathoth, though some critics prefer Jehoiachin
unknown: neither the time, nor the reign, nor the interval since the previous chapter can be determined

debates.question: What covenant is meant by the words of this covenant?

positions.view: the covenant entered into after the discovery of the lost book of the Law under Josiah, from which the phrase acquired a definite sense
the law of Moses itself, or the covenant at Horeb, or rather the one made in the land of Moab
the covenant of the law delivered by Moses, to which the people more than once promised obedience

outliers.reading: Alone makes something of the plural summons, taking it to show that a few colleagues remained who confirmed the prophet's doctrine, and that though he excelled them there was no emulation, since he willingly admitted all who were united in so good a cause.

Alone treats the curse as a mosaic of phrases taken with slight verbal changes from the recently discovered book of the Law, and explains the iron furnace as a smelter's furnace given special force by the brick-kilns of the bondage.

themes: The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying,
Hear ye the words of this covenant, and speak unto the men of Judah, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem;
And say thou unto them, Thus saith the Lord God of Israel; Cursed be the man that obeyeth not the words of this covenant,

4.pericope_label: Obey my voice, and ye shall be my people: yet they obeyed not, but walked every one in the imagination of his evil heart

schools.summary: Notices that the promised plenty is pastoral rather than agricultural and so belongs to Israel's earlier life, takes the prophet's answer for a liturgical Amen, and changes the tense of the closing threat from prediction to appeal.

Treats the land as only the pledge of a promise that already includes eternal life, imagines the objection the preaching would meet, and finds a legal figure in God submitting himself as it were to a third party's judgment.
Turns the Amen into a double petition, supposes the covenant read aloud in every city and street, and keeps the future threat where the grammarians would put a past tense.

debates.question: What does the prophet's Amen mean?

positions.view: the Amen of Israel's litanies, brought into fresh prominence by the newly found book and uttered at the solemn ceremony under Josiah
a double petition, that the promises be fulfilled and the incorrigible beware of the threatenings
either asserting the truth of what God had said, or wishing that the people would act according to their covenant

debates.question: Is the closing clause a prediction or a retrospect?

positions.view: a retrospect: read that God has brought these things upon them, so the words are an appeal to past experience as foreshadowing the future rather than a direct prediction
a prediction: God threatens to bring upon them all the words of threatening annexed to the covenant

outliers.reading: Alone stages the objection the preaching would meet, with the people protesting that they are the disciples of Moses, taught the law from childhood, and telling the prophet to take himself off to the Chaldeans or the Egyptians.
Alone observes that a land flowing with milk and honey describes the plenty of a pastoral rather than an agricultural people, and so belongs to the earlier stages of Israel's life.

themes: Which I commanded your fathers in the day that I brought them forth out of the land of Egypt, from the iron furnace, saying, Obey my voice, and do them, according to all which I command you: so shall ye be my people, and I will be your God:
That I may perform the oath which I have sworn unto your fathers, to give them a land flowing with milk and honey, as it is this day. Then answered I, and said, So be it, O Lord.
Then the Lord said unto me, Proclaim all these words in the cities of Judah, and in the streets of Jerusalem, saying, Hear ye the words of this covenant, and do them.
For I earnestly protested unto your fathers in the day that I brought them up out of the land of Egypt, even unto this day, rising early and protesting, saying, Obey my voice.

Yet they obeyed not, nor inclined their ear, but walked every one in the imagination of their evil heart: therefore I will bring upon them all the words of this covenant, which I commanded them to do; but they did them not.

9.pericope_label: A conspiracy is found among the men of Judah: according to the number of thy cities were thy gods, O Judah

schools.summary: Reads the conspiracy as literal politics, an organised secret resistance to Josiah's reforms that surfaced at his death, and gives the forefathers their stricter sense of the first fathers.

Presses the verb, so that the plot is discovered as thieves are caught in the act, argues that late apostasy is less excusable than early, and resolves how a people can cry to God and to idols at once.
Reduces the conspiracy to a figure for universal agreement in sin, recalls the reformation that was reversed, and traces the name of the idol through several languages.
Draws from the inescapable evil the rule that those who will not submit to God's government cannot escape his wrath, and notes the bitterness of men in affliction seeking a God they had slighted.

debates.question: Is the conspiracy an actual plot?

positions.view: yes, and a political one: an organised though secret resistance ran all through the reforming years and explains the rapid apostasy after Josiah's death
yes: they had become sworn brothers, determined to cast off the divine yoke and no longer have God reign over them
no: a figure only, since all sorts of people acted alike, as if they had conspired together to break the law
yes, and now proved: the thing has been discovered as thieves are caught in the very act, so it is no longer disputable that they perverted God's worship deliberately

debates.question: How can they cry to God and to idols together?

positions.view: because the unbelieving mind in a turbulent state turns here and there and lays hold of nothing fixed; they cry to God first and, unheard, turn to the others
the gods cried to are many because the name of the idol was a common one borne by every image set up in city and street

outliers.reading: Alone follows the relapse through to its cure, judging that it required a captivity to end the propensity, that God sent one, and that after it there was no idolatry among the Jews.

Alone makes the charge comparative, that the first fall into superstition was more excusable because they had not yet struck deep roots in true religion, so that relapse after many warnings is confirmed and hopeless obstinacy.

themes: And the Lord said unto me, A conspiracy is found among the men of Judah, and among the inhabitants of Jerusalem.

They are turned back to the iniquities of their forefathers, which refused to hear my words; and they went after other gods to serve them: the house of Israel and the house of Judah have broken my covenant which I made with their fathers.
Therefore thus saith the Lord, Behold, I will bring evil upon them, which they shall not be able to escape; and though they shall cry unto me, I will not hearken unto them.
Then shall the cities of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem go, and cry unto the gods unto whom they offer incense: but they shall not save them at all in the time of their trouble.

For according to the number of thy cities were thy gods, O Judah; and according to the number of the streets of Jerusalem have ye set up altars to that shameful thing, even altars to burn incense unto Baal.

14.pericope_label: Pray not thou for this people: what hath my beloved to do in mine house, a green olive tree, fair and of goodly fruit

schools.summary: Explains the ban on prayer as at once too early and too late, judges the difficult verse probably corrupt while holding its general sense clear, and reads the naming of the olive as the divine purpose in Israel's election.

Infers from the prohibition that the prophet had been praying all along, overturns the received construction of the beloved in favour of the Targum's, and asks whether the tree's beauty was ever its own.
Says only that their measure is full, takes the endearment straightforwardly of a people God had married, and notes that they gloried in the wickedness they were charged with.

debates.question: Who is my beloved, and who is speaking?

positions.view: God speaking of Judah as his betrothed, though the endearment is ironical; the received explanation that makes the prophet the speaker and the temple his house is simply wrong
Judah, or Israel collectively, as the betrothed of Jehovah, asking what part she has in the house she pollutes
God speaking of a people whose husband he formerly was
possibly the prophet, meaning that God has no business in a defiled sanctuary; or God speaking of the Jews, beloved for their fathers' sake
possibly Abraham or Moses, whose powerful intercession would now go unregarded; or else an endearment belonging to Israel as espoused to God

debates.question: What does the olive figure grant before it takes away?

positions.view: a genuinely noble planting, the fruit being the nation in its individual members, with the reversal introduced without any adversative particle and so the more abrupt and violent
the ideal Israel was meant to be and made no effort to become, the naming of the name expressing the purpose of her calling and election
nothing of her own: the beauty proceeded wholly from God's gratuitous kindness, so the planter may pull up his own tree when he pleases

outliers.reading: Alone declares the almost universally received explanation of the beloved to be mistaken, and says that anyone who considers the words wisely will wonder that so many learned men went wrong on a point by no means doubtful.

Alone judges the Hebrew of the verse probably corrupt, offers both a rendering and a conjectural emendation, and points out that the word translated lewdness means primarily a plan and then a scheme in a bad sense.

themes: Therefore pray not thou for this people, neither lift up a cry or prayer for them: for I will not hear them in the time that they cry unto me for their trouble.
What hath my beloved to do in mine house, seeing she hath wrought lewdness with many, and the holy flesh is passed from thee? when thou doest evil, then thou rejoicest.
The Lord called thy name, A green olive tree, fair, and of goodly fruit: with the noise of a great tumult he hath kindled fire upon it, and the branches of it are broken.

For the Lord of hosts, that planted thee, hath pronounced evil against thee, for the evil of the house of Israel and of the house of Judah, which they have done against themselves to provoke me to anger in offering incense unto Baal.

18.pericope_label: I was like a lamb brought to the slaughter: I will bring evil upon the men of Anathoth, even the year of their visitation

schools.summary: Reconstructs the sequence from threats to conspiracy, corrects the lamb from a noun to an adjective, and weighs the imprecation as belonging to an earlier stage of the religious life without hastily condemning it.
Explains the hatred as men assailing God's servants because they dare not assail God, and resolves the prophet's apparent inconsistency by distinguishing private feeling from zeal.

Derives the word for the lamb from a root meaning familiar and turns it on the townsmen who had bred him, softens the imprecation into a prediction, and notes that the conspiracy is recorded nowhere else.

Tells how the warning came when neither friend nor enemy would give it, observes that discovering the devices was defeating them, and answers what the enemies would have made of a prophet who could not foresee his own peril.

debates.question: How should the prayer for vengeance be judged?

positions.view: it is not a prayer at all: render it I shall see the punishment inflicted

it belongs to an earlier stage of the religious life, before indignation is tempered by forgiveness; not to be imitated, but not hastily condemned, since appealing to a higher judge is itself a victory over private revenge
some find human frailty in it and set Christ's contrary example against it, others a pure zeal for the glory of God
not inconsistent with his meekness: he disregarded his own life and was unmoved by private wrongs, but he was nevertheless not a log of wood, and zeal for God ate up his heart

debates.question: What is the force of the lamb the prophet compares himself to?

positions.view: a tame lamb reared in its master's house, the disjunctive being absent and an adjective mistaken for a noun; possibly an allusion to the sufferer of the earlier chapter
a lamb bred in the house and familiar with the family, from a cognate meaning accustomed, companion, intimate friend, which is exactly what the men of Anathoth had been to him
the disjunctive is absent, so the second word qualifies the first; the versions offer tame, harmless and clean

outliers.reading: Alone dwells on how the warning reached him, that none of his friends could and none of his enemies would give it, and that such were the devices that the discovering of them was the defeating of them.

Alone carries the motive into his own century, hearing in the townsmen's rage the same clamour that meets the reproof of hidden vices, when the profane demand to know who told the preacher and whether he has an oracle from heaven.

themes: And the Lord hath given me knowledge of it, and I know it: then thou shewedst me their doings.

But I was like a lamb or an ox that is brought to the slaughter; and I knew not that they had devised devices against me, saying, Let us destroy the tree with the fruit thereof, and let us cut him off from the land of the living, that his name may be no more remembered.
But, O Lord of hosts, that judgest righteously, that triest the reins and the heart, let me see thy vengeance on them: for unto thee have I revealed my cause.
Therefore thus saith the Lord of the men of Anathoth, that seek thy life, saying, Prophesy not in the name of the Lord, that thou die not by our hand:
Therefore thus saith the Lord of hosts, Behold, I will punish them: the young men shall die by the sword; their sons and their daughters shall die by famine:
And there shall be no remnant of them: for I will bring evil upon the men of Anathoth, even the year of their visitation.
